This research establishes the presence of self-similar solutions within the Yamabe flow, specifically under the condition of positive Yamabe type. The authors prove that within a suitable functional space, the flow admits a unique solution starting from any given self-admissible initial data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the long-time existence of this flow, showing it persists indefinitely.

In recent years, aspect-based recommendation has emerged as a significant research focus, aiming to capture user preferences by analyzing item attributes within user feedback. Nevertheless, existing methods often overlook the dynamic shifts in how users value specific item attributes across different contexts. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module designed to model these contextual variations in user preferences. Specifically, GAPE employs a dual gating mechanism to regulate the intensity of user preferences for distinct aspects, thereby enhancing the learning of user preference vectors. Empirical evaluations across two aspect-based recommendation benchmarks demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

We apply obstruction theory to analyze the space of weakly unital symplectic sheaves over a weakly associative symplectic stack, utilizing it to establish an extension of the Deligne hypercohomology theory.
We employ generating functions to analyze partition restrictions involving bounded part multiplicities, using this approach to derive several novel partition identities.

This study examines the weighted least squares approach for function approximation using a fixed set of exact data points. We demonstrate that stability and optimality can be simultaneously achieved by selecting a specific form of the weighting matrix. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the approximation error and illustrate how the proposed method relates to kernel-based techniques.

The internal structure of the X(3872) particle significantly impacts its reaction rates and initial conditions within hadronic interactions. We investigate the influence of various X(3872) configurations on the hadronic phase of the hadronization process, specifically examining how these models affect the particle's yield during the hadronic stage. Our findings indicate that the predicted X(3872) abundance is highly sensitive to the assumed internal structure of the X(3872) state.

The local moment behavior observed in disordered semiconductors like Si:P originates from the interaction between a localized electron and its hole. This study examines the influence of the electron-hole exchange interaction on the magnetic susceptibility of these local moments. We demonstrate that the exchange mechanism produces a distinct temperature dependence characterized by a low-temperature upturn in susceptibility. Furthermore, we show that the magnitude of this upturn is governed by the anisotropy of the electron-hole exchange interaction.
This paper establishes exchange relations for the GSO of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, demonstrating that these laws are intrinsically linked to the group's Coxeter length and descent set.

This study examines the implications of explicit symmetry breaking on the conservation of the U(1) current within a complex scalar field framework. We demonstrate that although the symmetry is not perfectly preserved due to explicit breaking terms, the associated current remains effectively conserved up to corrections of order O(ε), where ε represents the magnitude of the breaking parameter.

This study introduces a hierarchical Bayesian model designed to facilitate robot learning within real-world settings. By modeling confounding variables that hinder performance, the system automatically deduces their nature and eliminates their impact. Furthermore, the framework leverages prior knowledge to accelerate the acquisition of new skills. The efficacy of this approach is validated through simulations involving a mobile robot navigating an office environment.

This paper examines the space $\tilde{X}_H$, defined as the quotient of a topological space $X$ by a finite normal subgroup $H$ of the fundamental group $\pi_1(X)$, focusing on both the whisker and lasso topologies. We establish that these two topologies are equivalent on $\tilde{X}_H$ precisely when the whisker topology is Hausdorff. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the whisker topology yields a Hausdorff result if and only if the whisker topology on the universal cover $\tilde{X}$ is Hausdorff. Finally, we provide specific examples illustrating scenarios where the lasso topology fails to be Hausdorff.

Motion planning constitutes a critical component of autonomous driving, yet existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods often fail to leverage the capabilities of classical planning algorithms. This paper introduces a DRL framework for motion planning that explicitly utilizes the $A^*$ algorithm. Unlike conventional approaches, the system employs $A^*$ to generate a reward function rather than a direct solution, thereby enabling the DRL agent to learn an effective policy. Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid approach significantly outperforms both standard DRL techniques and $A^*$ itself in scenarios where optimal solutions are unattainable.

We investigate the potential of Eddington-regulated disk accretion onto a central black hole to explain the origin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs). Our findings indicate that such disks can supply the necessary mass growth over the typical lifespan of a starburst event. Furthermore, the resulting black hole mass is largely determined by the initial stellar mass formed within the disk. We also demonstrate that the characteristic mass of these SMBHs aligns well with the observed correlation between black hole mass and bulge stellar velocity dispersion (the $M_{\rm BH}-\sigma$ relation).

This paper introduces a novel framework for applying test-time training (TTT) to classification tasks using deep learning models. By leveraging an entropy-based uncertainty quantification method, the proposed approach refines classification outcomes through the iterative adjustment of class logits. Additionally, the study extends this technique to multi-label scenarios. Empirical evaluations across various benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances classification accuracy.

This study investigates the citation dynamics of papers released as preprints versus formal journal articles. Utilizing a dataset of 1,000 computer science manuscripts from arXiv that were eventually published in journals, we observed that articles accompanied by a preprint receive significantly more citations than those without. Furthermore, we found that the presence of a preprint accelerates the rate at which citations accumulate. Our findings indicate that preprints enhance both the volume and velocity of citations, likely by expediting access to research.

This paper introduces a web-based platform designed to streamline laboratory data management and documentation. By automatically generating documents from raw data, the system significantly minimizes human error. Furthermore, it offers robust security measures, including data encryption and access controls, to ensure the integrity and privacy of laboratory records.

Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly enhanced the prediction of material phase formations and mechanical properties, with applications extending to discovering new alloys and optimizing existing ones. However, these models often lack the interpretability required for practical use in fields like materials science. This study introduces a novel framework that combines a variational autoencoder with a random forest to generate both accurate and interpretable predictions. We validate this approach by testing it on two datasets: one concerning the phase stability of high-entropy alloys and another regarding the mechanical behavior of steel alloys.

This study investigates the strong decay mechanism of the $T_{cc}^{\tau+}$ particle into $D^{(\ast)}\bar{D}^{(\ast)}\tau$ final states, with a specific focus on final state interactions (FSI) arising from $D^{(\ast)}\bar{D}^{(\ast)}$ interactions and those involving the $\tau\nu_\tau$ pair. We demonstrate that contributions from $D^{(\ast)}\bar{D}^{(\ast)}$ FSI are substantial, whereas effects stemming from $D^{(\ast)}\bar{D}^{(\ast)}\tau\nu_\tau$ FSI are negligible. Consequently, our analysis of the $T_{cc}^{\tau+}$ decay spectrum incorporates these significant interaction terms.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone of machine learning, particularly for extracting features from graph-structured data. This study introduces a novel approach to subspace learning by utilizing GNNs to generate effective representations of nodes. We propose a new criterion for subspace learning that leverages the graph-driven node embeddings to minimize reconstruction error. The resulting optimization framework is solved through an iterative algorithm that alternates between updating the subspace projection and the corresponding basis. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm the method's superior performance relative to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper addresses the completeness problem concerning Sidon sets within the context of a limited Euclidean plane. We demonstrate that hyperbolic curves and elliptical paths serve as potent instruments for resolving this issue. Furthermore, we establish the existence of specific infinite sequences of complete $S$-sets within the finite Euclidean plane.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm for generating random binary matrices that approximates a specified rank, leveraging a non-uniform sampling distribution. We demonstrate theoretically that this distribution outperforms uniform sampling by significantly reducing the sampling variance of the resulting matrix's rank. Additionally, we provide empirical results confirming these findings and discuss the practical application of this approach to approximate matrix rank under a constraint of limited memory.

This study examines the fitting procedure for Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) across varying energy scales, specifically addressing the role of DGLAP evolution in this process. We demonstrate that PDF fitting can be reformulated as an equivalent fit for effective PDFs defined at the fitting scale, a form that does not rely on DGLAP evolution. By applying this methodology, we perform PDF fits at 2 GeV utilizing NNLO DGLAP evolved data and compare the outcomes with standard evolved PDFs. Our analysis reveals that the differences between these two approaches are negligible, thereby confirming that traditional PDF fitting using evolution equations remains valid.

This paper introduces enhancements to the open-source data mining library ELKI, which has been expanded with new algorithms, methods, and features. These developments significantly boost performance and scalability, while also elevating the quality of results.

We present a comprehensive theoretical framework for modeling microcombs driven by a modulated pump, specifically analyzing how sidebands influence spectral characteristics. By adapting the standard $\kappa$-$\gamma$-$\Omega$ model to incorporate multiple pump sidebands, we develop an analytical solution that reveals how spacing and amplitude of these sidebands affect the microcomb's spectrum. Our findings indicate that a broad spectrum of stable microcomb states can be achieved, with the ability to generate equidistantly spaced lines over a wide range of pump modulation frequencies. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectral properties of the microcomb can be precisely tailored by adjusting the relative amplitudes of the pump-sidebands.

This paper demonstrates that any finitely generated non-amenable group possesses a characteristic random subgroup that is both faithful and weakly mixing. Additionally, we prove that when a finitely generated group exhibits the property of being either hyperbolic or containing a free subgroup, its random subgroups are invariably isomorphic to the free group on countably many generators.

This study examines quasi neural networks (QNNs), which are defined as compositions of standard neural networks (NNs) where the layers are not necessarily weight-symmetric. We analyze the dynamics of QNNs through the lens of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), demonstrating that the NTK of a quasi NN can be expressed as a linear combination of the NTKs of its constituent NNs. Furthermore, we establish that the NTK of a quasi NN shares the same asymptotic decay rate as that of a standard NN. These findings are supported by the derivation of a closed-form solution for the evolution of the NTK of a quasi NN, which is expressed as a linear combination of the evolution equations of the individual component NTKs.

We demonstrate that imposing monogamy of mutual information on bulk entropies necessitates a corresponding monogamy constraint on the entropies of the boundary. This finding extends beyond the constraints provided by the Ryu-Takayanagi formula, which is not applicable to all scenarios. Additionally, we derive a specific condition that must be met by any valid holographic entropy monogamy relation.

We establish a connection between the local state probabilities of a specific class of solvable lattice models and the branching rule applicable to the associated symmetric powers of vector representations for $GL(n)$ and $GL(n+1)$. Consequently, these local probabilities can be formulated utilizing the coefficients found within this branching rule.

This study introduces a hybrid stabilization technique designed to enhance the convergence of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) when applied to $\ell_1$-regularized convex optimization problems. By integrating two distinct stabilization methods, the proposed approach leverages their combined benefits to achieve superior performance. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that this new algorithm outperforms both the standard ADMM and existing stabilized variants in terms of signal recovery efficacy.

This study evaluates the efficacy of various coaddition algorithms in creating consistent point-spread function (PSF) profiles for astronomical images. We applied these methods to the Deep Lens Imaging Survey (DLIS) data, which includes 12 filters from the Subaru Suprime-Cam instrument. Our analysis reveals that nonlinear approaches, such as clipped mean and median, do not yield a uniform PSF shape. Conversely, linear coaddition strategies produce a stable PSF profile that aligns well with the average profile of stellar images. Consequently, we advocate for the use of linear coaddition in DLIS data processing.

We establish the connection between the bounded chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa \in (0,4)$) and its dual, SLE$_{16/\textcolor{red}{-}\kappa}$, within an Im-holomorphic surface framework. This framework utilizes the height function $h = u + iv$, where $u$ and $v$ represent the harmonic components corresponding to the flow's driving terms. Specifically, we demonstrate that the pair of driving functions $(\xi_t, \eta_t)$ generated by the SLE$_\kappa$ process and its dual are jointly distributed as a time-changed two-dimensional Brownian motion.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations under the assumption of bounded initial data in $L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)$. We establish that the maximum norms of the solution and its derivatives grow at most logarithmically with time. Specifically, we prove that $\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)} \leq C(1 + \ln t)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)} \leq C(1 + \ln t)^{\frac{3}{2}}$ for all $t > 0$, where $C$ is a constant. These results improve upon previous estimates by Cao, Soghal, and Wu, which only demonstrated logarithmic growth for the solution itself. Our approach relies on a novel estimate for the $L^\infty$ norm of the gradient of the heat kernel, combined with a bootstrap argument applied to the parabolic structure of the heat equation.

We introduce a novel continuous-variable verification quantum circuit (CVQC) protocol designed for efficiently validating noisy, near-term variational quantum algorithms. This approach leverages a linear combination of single-qubit rotations to construct a measurement circuit that accelerates verification by an order of magnitude compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the protocol demonstrates robustness against coherent and incoherent errors, as well as Gaussian noise, ensuring reliable performance across diverse error models.

Recent breakthroughs in deep generative models have enabled the synthesis of complex images, including cells, with high fidelity. This paper demonstrates how these models can be leveraged to augment datasets for cell shape analysis, specifically improving performance in segmentation and tracking. We introduce a novel methodology for generating synthetic cell trajectories by integrating deep generative models with a new approach to synthesizing velocity fields. Empirical results indicate that this technique significantly enhances the efficacy of cell tracking and segmentation algorithms. The source code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/robinhessl/synthetic_trajectories.

Recent research in reinforcement learning has demonstrated that geometric capabilities can emerge spontaneously when agents are trained on non-geometric objectives. This study investigates how recurrent neural network (RNN) memory characteristics influence performance in these emergent geometric scenarios. We find that task success correlates with the sustained persistence of features within the network's hidden states. Furthermore, we show that modifying the temporal dynamics of both the network and its input stream can regulate this persistence, thereby offering a mechanism to control the emergence of geometric skills. These results provide fresh insights into the relationship between RNN memory traits and the development of geometric cognition.

We introduce a modified ECMC algorithm grounded in the Newtonian equations of motion, designed to overcome the limitations of the original method which suffers from dynamical arrest in three-dimensional dipolar systems. This variant demonstrates superior performance in generating equilibrium configurations for such models, enabling the investigation of dipolar glass states. By analyzing the system's behavior across various dipolar interaction strengths, we have identified the characteristic glass transition.

This study investigates the impact of data augmentation on sound event detection performance, specifically examining how different strategies influence the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. The authors evaluate various methods, including random masking, time masking, and the use of background sounds, alongside different inference approaches such as test-time augmentation and ensemble techniques. Findings indicate that test-time augmentation delivers superior results compared to ensemble methods. Furthermore, the combination of random masking with test-time augmentation emerges as the most effective strategy, offering the best balance of high accuracy and efficiency.

This study introduces a novel property termed "superposition" for information-theoretic quantities, with potential applications in fields such as federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We formally define superposition and establish its fundamental characteristics, including monotonicity, convexity, and a superposition principle. Furthermore, we demonstrate the property's practical utility by deriving non-orthogonal multiple access schemes that achieve optimal federated learning performance.

This paper introduces a novel framework for signal detection and estimation within spectrograms, grounded in the concept of level sets. We demonstrate that this approach yields a specialized form of the generalized likelihood ratio test and establishes the corresponding minimum distance estimator. Furthermore, we prove the consistency of this estimator and provide asymptotic results for the test. The study concludes by offering several illustrative examples to showcase the methodology.

This work introduces a novel approach to determine the count of synchronized clusters within a dynamical system. The methodology involves analyzing the rank of the system's adjacency matrix and determining the number of invariant manifolds that partition the system's state space. The validity of this theory is demonstrated through numerical simulations of both fully connected and scale-free networks composed of Lorenz oscillators.

This paper introduces a new module designed to simulate systems where bodies move according to Newton's laws of motion. It features a versatile, lightweight, and easy-to-use API that allows users to define custom forces and constraints. The module employs a time-stepping approach utilizing a generalized implicit integrator, which is solved via a nonlinear solver based on the Gauss-Newton method. Additionally, it incorporates a lightweight, fast explicit integrator for scenarios not requiring the solution of coupled equations. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through various examples, including a comparison of computational performance between the two integration methods.

We introduce a new class of information engines based on continuously monitored quantum systems. Unlike conventional methods, this framework utilizes measurement records to drive unitary system evolution, thereby enabling information-to-work conversion. We demonstrate the feasibility of extracting finite amounts of work through a simple model of a two-level system. Furthermore, we derive a generalized second law of thermodynamics applicable to this continuous measurement regime.

This study investigates the jamming transition of disks confined within a square channel, where each disk possesses a distinct weight. We demonstrate that varying the weight disparity between adjacent disks significantly alters the jamming process. Specifically, when the ratio of neighboring weights is small, the system undergoes a standard jamming transition; however, as this ratio increases, the transition shifts to a delayed onset. Furthermore, we observe that the critical value of the weight ratio required for this shift depends on the overall system size.

This study examines the precipitation variations across the United States linked to the three primary variants of El Niño and La Niña. Utilizing a Bayesian model selection framework, we evaluate the statistical significance of these patterns and determine their distinctiveness from one another. Our findings reveal that the different flavors of these climate events produce distinct precipitation outcomes, with significant implications for regional planning and forecasting.

We examine the mass spectra of black holes originating from Population III stars, considering both scenarios where massive black holes form from heavy seeds and where they grow from light ones. Our analysis reveals that the resulting mass spectra are largely independent of the initial formation mechanisms of these black holes. Instead, the final distributions are primarily determined by the accretion physics governing their subsequent evolution.

Multi-orbital flat bands are most prominent in kagome lattices, where they trigger significant correlation phenomena. This study examines the kagome Hubbard model featuring two orbitals per site, specifically analyzing the interplay between flat band-induced correlations and the Jahn-Teller distortion. We employ a variational Monte Carlo method to evaluate ground state properties, utilizing a Gutzwiller-projected wave function constructed from a linear combination of basis states. These states combine a Jahn-Teller distorted geometry with a wave function that is either spin-polarized or exhibits spin-singlet pairing. Our findings indicate that the system's ground state is best described by a spin-polarized configuration, a result that aligns with recent theoretical predictions.

Although protein sequence variations are known to impact phenotypic changes, the extent of this influence on specific phenotype-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) remains unclear. To investigate this, we analyzed 1,000 Genome European data for 19 traits, evaluating the correlation between each trait-linked SNP and the probability of the corresponding protein sequence occurring. Our findings reveal that the influence of protein sequences varies significantly across different traits, with the majority of SNPs showing no substantial connection to sequence probability. Furthermore, we observed that the likelihood of a SNP affecting a protein's structure or function correlates positively with the strength of the sequence association. Finally, we developed a novel method, termed "Protein Sequence Inference" (PSI), designed to identify protein sequences that maximize the correlation with a given trait.
This paper establishes that for any 2-design where the number of points is a prime power, its automorphism group must be solvable.

This study introduces a variational framework for calculating informational entropies within confined electronic systems. The proposed model is applicable to both ground and excited states, provided the trial wave function adheres to the necessary constraints. The resulting entropy variational principle is then utilized to demonstrate that, in low-dimensional confined electronic systems, positive informational entropies arise specifically from correlation effects, particularly Coulomb interactions.

This study introduces a novel method for measuring the velocity dispersion of wide binary stars using line-of-sight velocities, a technique that surpasses traditional approaches relying on proper motions. By applying this new framework to the Gaia Data Release 2 catalog, we identified 1,000 wide binaries with separations exceeding 1,000 astronomical units. Our analysis reveals that the median velocity dispersion for this group is 0.41 km/s, with a corresponding median orbital period of 1,000 years. Additionally, we examined the correlation between velocity dispersion and projected separation, finding that the dispersion increases with separation; however, this trend is partially attributed to measurement uncertainties. After correcting for these errors, the dispersion rises from 0.41 km/s at separations of 1,000 AU to 0.50 km/s at 10,000 AU. These findings align with previous studies and offer further support for the hypothesis that wide binaries are influenced by external tidal forces.

This paper introduces a novel category of ideal representations for proof structures within multiplicative linear logic, offering a fresh perspective on the inherent logical meaning of these elements. We demonstrate that these ideal representations possess sufficient expressive power to accommodate the interpretation of polarized proof structures augmented with non-standard connectives, specifically including the bang (!) and question (?).

This study investigates the application of deep learning for forecasting the synchronization between specific financial time series pairs. We introduce a novel approach that leverages the prediction accuracy of these models to estimate the degree of synchrony. Empirical results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in predicting synchronization, particularly when applied to certain data sets. Furthermore, utilizing this approach to construct a synchrony matrix enables the identification of latent structures within the data.

The interaction of vibrational modes with quantum states can significantly lower reaction barriers and enhance their control. We introduce a new theoretical framework for analyzing the coupling between two oscillating modes, specifically designed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of barrier suppression. This approach is applied to the prototypical $H_2O_2$ system, where it successfully accounts for the barrier reduction observed in its ground electronic state. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the barrier suppression in the excited electronic state arises from an analogous mechanism.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to enhance click-through rate prediction in online advertising by leveraging visual IDs. We posit that visual IDs offer valuable supplementary information regarding user interests and ad content. Accordingly, we develop an embedding layer dedicated to visual IDs and integrate it with a multi-task learning architecture. Empirical evaluations conducted on a real-world dataset demonstrate that this proposed model significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new formalism for business process management that incorporates cardinality constraints to regulate event sequence counts. Unlike previous approaches, this method allows for the concurrent execution of actions, a feature that significantly enhances process flexibility. The proposed approach utilizes a Petri net-based semantic framework to model these processes.

This study introduces a physics-informed statistical framework designed to model the Advanced Optical Detection (AOD) signal during wildfire smoke dispersion. The model integrates a statistical distribution for aerosol extinction coefficients with a physics-based equation governing the Beer-Lambert law of light attenuation. Parameter estimation employs a Bayesian methodology, utilizing data from a dual-wavelength lidar system. The methodology is validated using field data collected over a forest fire in California, demonstrating that the model effectively captures the primary characteristics of AOD profiles. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the proposed framework offers superior performance compared to traditional AOD inversion techniques.

This study introduces a new framework designed to mitigate privacy risks in location-based services (LBS) by addressing data dependent on user context. Unlike existing methods that overlook correlations between contextually linked datasets, this approach tackles associated privacy degradation. We propose a novel strategy for constructing multiple query sets that preserve privacy through the use of new context-aware differential privacy (CADP) mechanisms. Furthermore, we evaluate the framework's performance by analyzing query distribution patterns and location accuracy.

Functional connectivity (FC) is frequently assessed using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to investigate individual variations and inter-subject differences. However, the influence of inter-site factors on FC is often overlooked, despite evidence suggesting that such elements can compromise the detection of these differences. This study examines the impact of inter-site effects on FC by analyzing resting-state fMRI data from 1,020 participants sourced from the Human Connectome Project. We employed a rigorous methodology involving two distinct sites, two scanners, and two preprocessing pipelines to evaluate reliability. Our findings indicate that while inter-site effects are substantial, they do not significantly hinder the ability to identify group-level disparities. Conversely, these effects severely undermine the consistency of distinguishing individual subjects. Specifically, we observed that FC alterations linked to site and preprocessing methods are often negatively correlated with genuine FC differences between individuals. These results underscore the critical necessity of controlling for inter-site effects when conducting individual-level FC analyses.

This paper examines heat flow and its connection to concentration of measure inequalities. We demonstrate that a specific form of these inequalities holds if and only if the heat flow exhibits a corresponding ultracontractive behavior. Additionally, we provide a proof of these characterizations utilizing an approach based on flow interpolation.

Code-switching, the blending of multiple languages in text, is a prevalent linguistic phenomenon. Although recent advancements in natural language processing have largely focused on single-language inputs, there is growing interest in developing effective models for code-mixed text. This study introduces a novel approach leveraging positional encoding techniques to enhance language models specifically for code-mixed data. We evaluate this method using two distinct datasets: one featuring code-switched Hindi-English news articles and another containing raw, unstructured Hindi-English social media posts. The results demonstrate that this proposed approach consistently outperforms standard baseline configurations.

Utilizing density functional theory, we examine the isotope effect in hydrogen sulfide (H$_{3}$S) at elevated pressures. Our findings reveal that the total isotope factor ($\alpha$) comprises two components: a pressure-dependent electronic contribution ($\alpha_{e}$) and a pressure-independent nuclear term ($\alpha_{n}$). We observe that $\alpha_{e}$ rises from 0.002 to 0.004 across the 150–250 GPa range, whereas $\alpha_{n}$ remains constant at 0.017. Consequently, the combined coefficient ($\alpha$) spans 0.019 to 0.021 at these pressures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnitude of $\alpha_{e}$ is governed by the compressibility of the electronic structure, with its value correlating directly to the rate of change in H$_{2}$S's superconducting critical temperature ($T_{c}$) relative to hydrogen sulfide's ($T_{c}$) change.

In evolutionary biology, the average impact of gene substitutions on phenotype is frequently used to estimate phenotypic change. However, this approach often fails to capture the full picture because it overlooks the majority of substitutions that are neutral or deleterious. This study demonstrates that, under specific conditions, the total effect of substitutions can be predicted by average impacts alone. These conditions arise when the distribution of substitution effects remains consistent over time and when the probability of a specific substitution depends solely on the effect's magnitude. Under these constraints, the probability of a particular effect size determines the substitution rate, rendering the average effect a reliable proxy for overall phenotypic evolution. The paper further shows that this framework applies broadly, including to scenarios where fitness landscapes are smooth and genes function independently.

This study introduces a novel, model-based, closed-loop feedback strategy for bipedal robots that integrates both open- and closed-loop dynamics throughout the entire gait cycle. The proposed algorithm synchronizes the timing of stance and swing phases, while simultaneously generating model-predictive trajectories for leg movement and whole-body dynamics. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on a bipedal robot, highlighting its robustness against external disturbances and inaccuracies in system modeling.

Learned descriptors have significantly advanced various computer vision tasks, including image matching and camera pose estimation. Nevertheless, their application in pose estimation remains limited to specific scenarios, such as those involving high-quality inputs or large datasets. This paper introduces a novel, lightweight learned descriptor designed to enhance the performance of the RANSAC algorithm in estimating camera poses, particularly under challenging conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches in both accuracy and speed, successfully enabling precise and rapid pose estimation in difficult environments.

Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a promising privacy-preserving approach for distributed machine learning, yet existing methods often fail to adequately address heterogeneity among clients. This study introduces a personalized semi-supervised FL framework designed to handle data distribution disparities while leveraging unlabeled information. By establishing a semi-supervised learning model tailored to each client, the proposed system enhances performance, particularly for those possessing scarce labeled data. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a novel label correction mechanism to improve the utilization of unsupervised data. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches in both standard FL and scenarios involving heterogeneous data distributions.

We investigate the evolution of magnetic fields within neutron star (NS) disks formed following binary NS mergers, utilizing magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Our findings indicate that the disk's magnetic field intensifies rapidly post-disruption, reaching strengths of $10^{14}$ G within 100 ms. This growth is driven by the $\alpha$-effect, which operates in conjunction with the winding of the field by differential rotation. The resulting field evolution significantly influences the disk's thermal and viscous properties, as well as the dynamics of the outflow. Specifically, the outflow transitions from a viscous wind to a magnetically driven one, with mass ejection rates reaching $10^{-3} M_{\odot}$ s$^{-1}$ and velocities of approximately $0.1c$. These results demonstrate that magnetic fields play a critical role in shaping the post-merger system and must be incorporated into future models of disk evolution.

We introduce a novel, explicit formula for the initial Mumford-Morita-Miller class of a compact Riemann surface, leveraging the period matrix and the Hodge metric defined on the surface's canonical theta functions.

This study examines Markov processes defined on open metric spaces that exhibit absorption at the boundary. We establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing a unique quasi-stationary distribution with exponential decay, alongside the existence of an absorbing measure. Additionally, we demonstrate that the associated Markov process is Feller and strong Feller. These findings are illustrated through applications involving diffusion processes on manifolds with boundaries and branching processes.

This study investigates the equilibrium configurations of dielectric particles within a graphene waveguide, which is chemically doped to modify the zero-point fluctuations of the ground state. By adjusting the chemical potential of the graphene, the positions of the dielectric particles can be controlled. The derived analytical expressions for the Casimir force and its associated energy are applicable to any dielectric particle, regardless of its size or permittivity. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed setup offers a viable mechanism for trapping and manipulating dielectric particles.

This study investigates how variations in Emergency Department (ED) treatment durations influence patient outcomes, specifically focusing on 30-day revisit and readmission rates. Utilizing a quasi-experimental design, the analysis leverages exogenous fluctuations in treatment time to measure their impact. Findings indicate that extending treatment time by 30 minutes correlates with a 0.1 percentage point increase in 30-day revisits and a 0.03 percentage point increase in 30-day readmissions. Furthermore, the study examines how treatment time interacts with patient characteristics, revealing that the effect of additional time is more pronounced for elderly individuals and those with lower socioeconomic status.

This study investigates how agents with bounded rationality select task difficulties within a multi-agent environment. We demonstrate that when task difficulties are uniformly distributed, agents adopt a simple threshold rule, whereas non-uniform distributions lead to complex, non-linear decision strategies. Furthermore, we show that these complex strategies can be approximated by simpler rules, and this finding holds true even in scenarios involving multiple agents tackling tasks with varying difficulty levels.

We introduce a novel technique for analyzing charge-dependent two-particle correlations that effectively mitigates background influences tied to local charge conservation. This approach is applied to proton-lead collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair of 5.02 TeV, utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC. The study examines correlations involving negatively charged particles within the transverse momentum range of 0.15 to 2.0 GeV/c and positively charged particles between 0.2 and 2.0 GeV/c. The findings are contrasted with proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV, where the transverse momentum ranges for negative and positive particles are 0.2–2.0 GeV/c and 0.2–2.0 GeV/c, respectively.

This study investigates the predictive capabilities of crowd dynamics within Kickstarter, a prominent crowdfunding platform. We evaluate whether the behavioral traits of project creators and the dynamics of project development offer superior insights into funding success compared to project attributes and the characteristics of their creators. Our findings indicate that crowd dynamics are more predictive than static project or creator profiles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the features derived from crowd dynamics hold greater significance than those from project or creator data in forecasting outcomes.

This study introduces a decentralized deep learning framework for network intrusion detection, enabling organizations to collaborate on model training without compromising their private data. By employing federated learning, the proposed approach ensures privacy, allowing the sharing of model updates rather than raw data. Furthermore, the system addresses scenarios where data distribution is non-i.i.d. across different organizations. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to both centralized deep learning models and existing federated learning techniques.

This paper introduces an algorithm designed to optimize task execution by dynamically adjusting the sequence of operations based on the robot's current state. By leveraging a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework, the proposed method generates a conditional task sequence tailored to specific robot states, thereby enhancing efficiency. The authors validate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations involving a dual-arm robot performing a pick-and-place operation.

The mobility of a device is significantly influenced by the interface between the semiconductor and its gate materials. This study examines the mobility of silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge) when interfaced with various high-$\kappa$ dielectrics, including $\mathrm{HfO_2}$, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{La_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{Y_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{Gd_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{Lu_2O_3}$, and $\mathrm{Sc_2O_3}$. Utilizing density functional theory (DFT) and effective mass theory (EMT), we calculated the band offsets and effective mass parameters for these systems. The findings indicate that Si mobility is largely independent of the specific high-$\kappa$ material used, whereas Ge mobility shows a marked dependence on the choice of dielectric. Furthermore, the study identifies $\mathrm{Lu_2O_3}$ and $\mathrm{Gd_2O_3}$ as the optimal dielectrics for enhancing Ge mobility.

This study investigates the stability of group synchronization within networks composed of heterogeneous oscillators subject to small parameter variations. By utilizing a novel decomposition technique, we establish that the stability of group synchronization can be analyzed through the lens of the zero-state convergence of the corresponding linearized error dynamics. Specifically, we demonstrate the stability of group synchronization for both directed and undirected topologies by proving the existence of an appropriate Lyapunov function. The findings indicate that, given sufficiently minor parameter discrepancies, the rate of convergence toward group synchronization remains essentially unchanged compared to the homogeneous case.

This study investigates the prevalence of YouTube within the search results of various Western search engines. The findings reveal a consistent pattern where YouTube appears in the top results for nearly all queries, with its prominence increasing over time. The research further suggests that this widespread presence stems from a combination of factors, including the platform's extensive content library, its sophisticated recommendation algorithms, and its strategic partnerships with major advertisers.

We investigate the behavior of the $\Gamma$-function within two-dimensional conformal field theories featuring general monodromy defects. Our findings indicate that this function corresponds to that of an effectively theory-free system characterized by a modified coupling constant. Additionally, we derive a universal formula for the contribution of such defects to the conformal anomaly.

This paper investigates elliptic curves defined over a cubic Galois extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ that possess a rational point of order 13. We establish that such curves correspond to specific orbits of points of order 13 located on the curve $y^2 = x^3 - x$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit construction for $K$ and determine the corresponding Weierstrass equations. Finally, we outline the methodology used to verify these findings.

This study examines the local delay mechanism, a straightforward yet prevalent approach for regulating congestion in networks. The analysis focuses on the dynamic behavior of delay, which is computed based on the most recent packet inter-arrival times. The authors define three distinct operational regimes based on local delay levels: the stable regime, characterized by constant delay; the oscillatory regime, marked by periodic delay variations; and the chaotic regime, featuring unpredictable delay fluctuations. The paper investigates the conditions under which the system transitions between these regimes and demonstrates that the delay dynamics can be modeled using a one-dimensional map. Furthermore, the study reveals that the system's global behavior is governed by a bifurcation diagram, which is notably similar to that of the logistic map.

Semi-supervised Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) leverage graph structures to enhance node classification, yet they depend on the quality of their initial label predictions. Traditional pseudo-labeling approaches often generate noisy outputs that degrade GNN performance. This study introduces a novel method to improve the reliability of pseudo-labels by integrating uncertainty estimation with a self-training framework. Specifically, we utilize a Monte Carlo Dropout-enhanced GNN to assess prediction confidence, which then guides the selection of high-confidence samples for the subsequent training phase. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces PatchNet, a lightweight CNN designed for video object detection that surpasses existing efficient models like MobileNetV2 in both accuracy and speed. The architecture leverages a novel patch-based methodology, utilizing small input segments to enhance feature extraction. Additionally, we present a new loss function, $L_{\text{patch}}$, which improves performance by mitigating the impact of noisy labels. Comprehensive evaluations across three datasets—THUMOS14, ActivityNet, and MSR-VVD—demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art lightweight models.

We examine the discrete-time TASEP under arbitrary initial conditions, demonstrating that its multi-point distributions are governed by determinantal processes. By employing a technique of "freezing" particles at specific time instances, we establish links between the multi-point correlations of this discrete system and those of the continuous-time TASEP found in prior research. Consequently, this approach yields novel findings for systems starting from stepped initial configurations.

This study investigates the antenna-switching (AS) protocol within simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) environments, where users harvest energy from base station signals. We introduce a Generalized Antenna-Switching (GAS) method that optimizes the allocation of time and antennas to maximize system energy efficiency (EE). The resulting optimization framework is non-convex; however, we develop a generalized alternating optimization (AO) approach to iteratively address the problem. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity, suboptimal scheme for practical implementation. Simulation results demonstrate that the suboptimal method achieves performance nearly identical to the AO approach and significantly outdoes traditional time-switching techniques.

We introduce a novel perturbation theory for SU(N) fermions that yields the exact result as its second-order calculation. This framework is subsequently broadened to incorporate a scalar field, maintaining the feature of exact convergence at the second order.

This study introduces a novel framework for modeling quantum optomechanical systems, one that bridges the gap between traditional classical circuit representations and standard quantum formalisms. We demonstrate that when occupation numbers are substantial, this circuit-based approach yields results consistent with standard quantum theory, thereby enabling the extension of established circuit techniques to a broader spectrum of optomechanical configurations.

This study examines the generation of the generalised sextic Freud weight, which extends the well-known generalised Airy weight by incorporating a Gaussian factor. The paper presents the explicit formulas for the corresponding orthogonal polynomials and their corresponding moments. Additionally, it derives the differential equations satisfied by these polynomials and constructs the associated Stieltjes continued fraction.

This study investigates how the field of view (FOV) of a distance sensor influences the trajectory of an autonomous wall-following robot. By employing a linearized model of the robot's motion, we derive an analytical expression for the trajectory and demonstrate that the sensor's FOV dictates the resulting path. The analysis further reveals that specific combinations of control parameters and sensor FOV can generate limit cycles, a finding validated through numerical simulations.

In perturbative algebraic quantum field theory, selecting a Cauchy surface is essential for defining the relevant algebras. This work investigates how such choices influence the resulting algebra structures, demonstrating that algebras constructed on different Cauchy surfaces are locally isomorphic.

This study introduces a novel approach for classifying smoke and non-smoke imagery within surgical settings. The methodology employs a ResNet-50 backbone to extract features, which are subsequently processed by a Support Vector Machine (SVM) for binary decision-making. Experimental evaluations conducted on a custom dataset demonstrate the efficacy of this technique, achieving an accuracy of 98.2%, an F1-score of 98.1%, and a recall rate of 98.1%.

We introduce a novel design for frequency-robust Mølmer-Sørensen gates that significantly lowers entanglement buildup by reducing the reliance on high-order Bessel functions. This approach enhances gate fidelity and accelerates execution speed, particularly in systems featuring long ion chains.

This study investigates the interplay between equilibrium lattice parameters and filler A-cation size in inducing off-center displacements of the B-site cation within perovskite structures. Utilizing density functional theory (DFT), we analyzed a series of CsPbBr₃₋ₓClₓ and CsPbBr₃₋ₓIₓ solid solutions alongside the insertion of methylammonium (MA⁺) or formamidinium (FA⁺) ions. Our analysis reveals that both the equilibrium volume and the size of the A-site cation significantly influence B-cation off-centering; specifically, increasing the perovskite's equilibrium volume or employing a larger cation (such as FA⁺ relative to MA⁺) results in reduced B-site displacement. Furthermore, we examined the impact of varying the B-site halide composition (Cl vs. I) on these effects. The findings demonstrate that the magnitude of B-cation off-centering is primarily dictated by the perovskite's equilibrium volume and filler cation identity, rather than the specific type of halide anion.

Multivariate Gaussian processes (GPs) are frequently employed to model functions across multiple dimensions, where the output at any input vector is represented as a vector. In this study, we establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the graphical structure of the covariance matrix for a set of independent multivariate Gaussian processes remains consistent with a specified undirected graph. By enforcing conditional independence constraints between distinct processes, we guarantee that the resulting graphical covariance aligns with the target graph structure. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm capable of generating Gaussian processes whose correlations are compatible with any given graph.

We introduce a recurrent structure for quantum circuits designed to efficiently calculate ground state properties of molecular electronic states. By repeatedly applying a shallow unitary transformation to an initial guess, this method converges to the ground state. We demonstrate that utilizing these recurrent patterns significantly accelerates convergence compared to non-recurrent architectures. Furthermore, we prove that the recurrent quantum circuit (RQC) offers superior expressivity relative to both the VQE and VQCI approaches.

This study examines the average-case performance of the Generalized Chebyshev method, a second-order optimization algorithm, when applied to quadratic problems featuring a structured, positive-definite Hessian. We derive closed-form expressions for the average convergence behavior of this method and demonstrate that it outperforms classical first-order approaches, such as gradient descent, by achieving a quadratic improvement in average-case complexity. Furthermore, we establish lower bounds for average-case optimization under the constraints of second-order oracle access, proving that the Generalized Chebyshev method attains optimality within this framework.

Moiré heterostructures are renowned for their exotic electronic properties, which are anticipated to extend into their excitonic regimes. This study employs a many-body Green's function approach to investigate optical spectra involving interlayer excitons in moiré systems. We demonstrate that the interlayer binding energy significantly influences spectral features, a factor that must be accounted for to accurately describe experimental observations. Furthermore, we predict a pronounced blue shift in excitonic peaks driven by increased carrier density, a phenomenon arising from reduced interlayer binding energy. These findings offer valuable insights for interpreting current experimental data and guiding future research in this field.

This paper introduces an adaptive probabilistic data association (PDA) algorithm designed to enhance position estimation for mobile agents navigating dynamic environments. By integrating a computationally efficient method for estimating the probability of target existence, the system dynamically adjusts the association probability based on the target's motion characteristics. Furthermore, the algorithm employs a novel approach to calculate the covariance of the estimation error. Simulation results demonstrate that this method outperforms the conventional fixed-covariance PDA algorithm in both accuracy and efficiency.

This study reports the measurement of $W^\pm$ and $Z$ boson polarization using proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}=7$ and $13$ TeV, collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC with integrated luminosities of 5.0 fb$^{-1}$ and 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ respectively. The analysis focuses on events featuring a $W^\pm$ or $Z$ boson decaying into an electron and its corresponding neutrino, accompanied by at least one additional jet. Joint helicity fractions are determined for the boson's polarization states ($\lambda=0,\pm1$) by analyzing the angular distribution of the leptons and the boson's transverse momentum. The resulting measurements are compared against Standard Model predictions. Specifically, the observed joint helicity fractions align well with theoretical expectations.

We demonstrate that the Cotton tensor's zero value signifies the vacuum state of a scalar theory featuring a non-linear realization of symmetry. This finding is achieved by establishing an equivalence between the Cotton tensor and a specific Wess-Zumino (WZ) term within an odd-dimensional bulk, thereby confirming its role as a WZ term in that context.

We introduce a novel category of orthomodular spaces and establish their equivalence with orthomodular lattices. This framework further facilitates the formulation of a categorical equivalence between certain orthomodular spatial collections and complete atomic orthocomplemented posets.

We introduce a novel approach to automatically generating and assessing formal proofs. First, we generate proof representations using a proof assistant, then evaluate them with a verifier. By comparing the output of the verifier against the generated proofs, we can automatically identify errors. This feedback loop allows for the correction of flawed proofs, making the process suitable for integration into continuous integration systems or review workflows.

This paper investigates the Watson formula and the associated methods pioneered by Soundararajan and Harold G. Harper, which are instrumental in analyzing low-order moments of L-functions. We demonstrate the applicability of these techniques to specific families of L-functions that are amenable to explicit computation.

This paper introduces a novel early termination strategy for inner loops within interior point methods (IPMs) designed to enhance computational efficiency. By halting inner iterations before full convergence, the approach reduces the total count of inner steps required to solve the primary optimization problem. The authors rigorously analyze the efficacy of this technique and demonstrate that it maintains the global convergence properties of standard IPMs. Furthermore, numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method significantly accelerates IPM performance.

This study examines the transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$, which converts quark distribution from the fixed flavor number scheme to the variable flavor number scheme up to order $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$. The analysis employs the Mellin transform technique, utilizing the Laplace transform method to numerically invert the results.

The AI Incident Database (Databse) serves as a centralized repository for reports on AI system failures, designed to facilitate learning and improvement within the AI community. By offering a searchable collection of incidents, it enables researchers to identify patterns and derive actionable insights for refining intelligent systems. This paper details the database's architecture, its implementation, and the analytical methods employed to examine its data.

We introduce a differential equation for the Effective Action (ERG) that maintains manifest gauge invariance in Yang-Mills theory. This framework allows us to demonstrate that the ERG differential equation can be reformulated as a closed system involving only one-particle-irreducible (1PI) quantities.

This paper introduces a monitoring framework designed to observe the runtime behavior of processes defined by multiple LTSM (Labelled Transition System with Timers) models. The system generates alerts whenever observed actions conflict with one or more of the provided process models. A key feature is its ability to handle conflicts between specifications by prioritizing them based on assigned weights. The authors present an algorithm that constructs a specialized, time-aware monitoring automaton capable of efficiently tracking process compliance.

Proto-Quipper-M is Proto-Quipper's extended variant, designed to model the full capabilities of Proto-Quipper-M, including the creation of quantum circuits. This extended framework enforces the quantum no-cloning principle by ensuring that circuit instances remain independent and isolated from one another. To achieve this isolation, the authors employ a context-aware type system that tracks the usage of every quantum wire throughout the circuit. They further demonstrate the type safety of Proto-

We introduce a universal finite-size scaling framework designed to analyze the statistical distribution of eigenvalues in various random-matrix models. This approach leverages the concept of a canonical ensemble, where eigenvalues function as a one-dimensional gas of interacting particles. By examining the interactions among these particles, we derive a general expression for the scaling of the $n$-point eigenvalue correlation functions. Additionally, we present an illustrative example demonstrating the application of this method to the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble.

We introduce a quantum-enhanced method for detecting an optical phase using two-mode squeezing. This approach involves mixing the squeezed state with a coherent beam on a balanced homodyne detector. We demonstrate that the phase can be estimated with a variance reaching the two-mode squeezing level, surpassing the standard shot-noise limit.

Multiway number partitioning serves as a fundamental challenge in genomic sequence assembly, where it is used to merge multiple DNA fragments into a continuous sequence. This study introduces a novel algorithm for constructing a minimum-weight solution to the k-way partitioning problem, leveraging a new data structure called the k-heap. We demonstrate that this algorithm runs in $O(n \log n)$ time and occupies $O(n)$ space, where $n$ represents the total weight of the input numbers. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed method against current state-of-the-art approaches through extensive experiments on both randomly generated datasets and real-world data.

This study introduces a novel delayed logistic equation designed to model cell population dynamics. The analysis demonstrates that this equation guarantees convergence to a positive equilibrium, a property that aligns with experimental observations. Furthermore, the paper proposes a new, more efficient numerical method for solving this equation, supported by numerical results that validate its superior performance.

This study introduces a new transformation method for analyzing event times within point processes. By converting the original data into a multivariate normal distribution, it enables the application of standard statistical tools. The authors demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a simulation experiment and a real-world analysis of the first occurrence of Alzheimer's disease symptoms.

Hybrid quantum systems, which integrate superconducting and semiconductor components, are essential for advancing quantum technologies. These devices are distinguished by their capacity to generate, manipulate, and detect entangled Cooper pairs alongside electron spin states. This review examines the principles governing hybrid quantum conductors, with a specific emphasis on the generation and control of electron spin entanglement. We also explore the potential applications of these systems within quantum technologies.

The nuclear structure of nickel and germane isotopes around neutron number 40 has been examined using the shell model, with particular attention to the structural evolution across this region. This study highlights a marked shift in nuclear properties as one transitions from nickel to germanium isotopes at N=40. Furthermore, the observed evolution of nuclear structure within the germane isotopic chain is analyzed in detail.

Normalizing flows offer a powerful framework for modeling complex probability distributions by transforming simple base distributions through a series of invertible transformations. This work introduces a method for incorporating gauge symmetries into the U(1) theory of normalizing flows. By leveraging the inherent diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral, we construct a flow that remains equivariant under U(1) transformations. This approach allows for the systematic integration of gauge symmetry directly into the flow architecture. We validate this technique by applying it to a charged particle system, demonstrating its efficacy.

Biasing enhances the accuracy of recognizing text that adheres to specific formats by incorporating a bias term into the standard CTC loss function. This bias term increases scores for valid output sequences while decreasing scores for invalid ones. This paper introduces a biasing method that leverages the bias term to improve the recognition of text conforming to particular formats.

This study reports a measurement of single top quark production via the t-channel at the LHC, utilizing 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV gathered by the CMS experiment. The analysis focuses on events containing a lepton (either an electron or muon) and jets, with the cross section determined as 19.9 $\pm$ 1.1 (statistical) $\pm$ 1.1 (systematic) pb. This result aligns well with predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at next-to-next-to-leading order. Furthermore, the study investigates the consistency of the measured data with the hypothesis of a single top quark coupling to the W boson through a purely left-handed interaction; the findings support this standard model framework.

This study introduces a novel framework designed to enhance the precision of executing database queries without access to underlying data. By leveraging a trained neural network, the system predicts the optimal sequence of join operations for a given query. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts execution accuracy even when database contents are unknown.

We present the angular clustering statistics for galaxies from the first data release of the Low Frequency Array Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS DR1), covering the entire sky above |b| > 20° with a 2.5 Jy flux density limit. The analysis focuses on the angular two-point correlation function and the angular power spectrum, revealing that the observed clustering is consistent with predictions from the ΛCDM cosmological model. The study identifies a significant dependence of clustering strength on galaxy flux density, a trend that aligns with expectations from the luminosity function. Additionally, we examine the angular clustering of the brightest 2.5 Jy sources, finding that their distribution is well-described by a two-halo model.

The rank lasso problem involves minimizing a sum of squared errors and a non-differentiable, convex rank penalty, a formulation widely applicable in various statistical contexts. Although prior research has largely focused on low-dimensional scenarios, this study addresses the high-dimensional case where the number of features exceeds the sample size. We introduce an adaptive-sieving-based algorithm capable of handling these dimensions efficiently. The paper further establishes the convergence of this proposed method and provides numerical experiments demonstrating its effectiveness.

We demonstrate that, within a broad class of quantum Markovian open systems, there exists a single, globally optimal strategy for entropy generation. This finding extends previous work by Attal, Fagnola, and Obata, which established only the existence of an optimal protocol for entropy production rates. We further prove that this global optimum is attainable, showing convergence of an iterative algorithm designed to achieve it.

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) serves as a robust framework for evaluating the environmental impacts of AI services, yet its application remains limited due to the complexity of data requirements. This paper introduces a streamlined LCA methodology specifically designed for AI services, demonstrating its efficacy through a case study of a sentiment analysis model. By applying this approach, we quantify the carbon footprint associated with the model's lifecycle, thereby offering a practical pathway for integrating LCA into AI development.

Prescriptive process monitoring (PPM) offers a data-driven approach to not only detect and diagnose deviations in business processes but also to prescribe optimal remedial actions. Although PPM has been extensively validated in controlled simulation environments, its efficacy in real-world scenarios remains largely unproven. This paper addresses that gap by validating PPM methods using actual data from a hospital setting. We evaluate the proposed actions through a combination of quantitative and qualitative analyses, ultimately demonstrating the method's practical viability and highlighting promising avenues for future research.

This study introduces a novel, unified framework for estimating and adapting errors in multiscale fluid-structure interaction problems. The approach integrates a dual-weighted residual (DWR) method with a specific technique for assessing interface coupling discrepancies. The framework's validity is demonstrated through applications to two cases: incompressible flow interacting with elastic solids and porous media flow interacting with elastic solids.

Graph packing involves selecting edge-disjoint copies of a specific subgraph $H$ from a host graph $G$ to maximize the total number of $H$ instances included. This problem is notoriously difficult, particularly regarding vertex-disjoint paths, where deriving tight bounds is challenging. This study introduces a novel framework for establishing lower bounds on the maximum packing of $H$ in $G$ by leveraging the structural properties of both graphs. We demonstrate that this approach yields tight bounds for the vertex-disjoint paths problem and extends effectively to other graph classes.

This study examines opinion dynamics within a one-dimensional framework where agents are divided into two groups, each characterized by a distinct opinion vector. The system's evolution is governed by a non-linear differential equation that incorporates both within-group cohesion and between-group repulsion. The analysis demonstrates that the system's long-term behavior is determined by the initial configuration, resulting in the spontaneous formation of social cliques. Furthermore, the paper provides a rigorous proof of the global existence and uniqueness of the system's trajectories.

Recent investigations into how black holes with scalar hair influence the dynamics of holographic superconductors have revealed that the former's traits are a subset of the latter's. This study extends those findings by examining the impact of scalar field self-interaction on the ground state of the system. We demonstrate that the properties of the zero-temperature state in the standard model align with those of the minimally coupled variant, whereas at finite temperatures, the two models exhibit distinct characteristics.

This study introduces a stochastic model designed to examine the production of mature messenger RNA (mRNA) in eukaryotic cells. The model incorporates the effects of chromatin structure, transcriptional dynamics, and nuclear splicing mechanisms. Our findings indicate that the temporal gap between the conclusion of transcription and the emergence of functional mRNA scales proportionally with gene length. Furthermore, we have developed a simplified, reduced-order model that effectively captures the statistical properties of mRNA abundance.

The evolution of excitation energy in the $^{64}$Ni nucleus is examined in relation to the neutron $N=40$ subshell gap and the monopole interaction. The study utilizes the interacting boson model (IBM) to derive the magnitude of the $^{64}$Ni subshell gap, yielding a value of 0.8 MeV. Additionally, the paper investigates the connection between the subshell gap and the monopole interaction, demonstrating that the former can be determined from the latter.

This study examines anomalies within SU(N) gauge theories featuring N Weyl fermions in the fundamental representation alongside an arbitrary number of adjoint Weyl fermions. We demonstrate that introducing even a single additional adjoint fermion renders all anomalies traceless, thereby ensuring the theory remains anomaly-free. Furthermore, we establish that these SU(N) theories with N fundamental and one or more adjoint fermions are dual to specific Sp(2M) gauge configurations. Specifically, these duals consist of Sp(2M) fundamental fermions augmented by additional adjoint Weyl fermions, where the parameter M is determined by the count of the original SU(N) adjoint fermions.

This paper examines group codes defined over the direct product of two cyclic groups, $C_{p^k} \times C_{pk}$, where $p$ is a prime and $k \geq 1$. We establish that the code $D^{\perp \perp}$ is equivalent to code $C$.
